value.overview: The Flesh-footed Shearwater is a medium to large oceanic seabird of the Indo-Pacific. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed on islands in Australia, New Zealand, and nearby regions. Its dark plumage, pale bill with a dark tip, and pinkish or flesh-colored feet distinguish it from many other shearwaters. The species is an uncommon visitor far from its usual range, including a documented record in Costa Rican Pacific waters.
value.classification: The Flesh-footed Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and the family Procellariidae, which includes shearwaters, petrels, and fulmars. Its scientific name is Ardenna carneipes.
value.identification: This shearwater has dark brown to blackish upperparts and generally dark underparts, with some paler areas on the face, throat, and underwing. The bill is pale horn-colored with a contrasting dark tip, while the legs and feet are distinctly pinkish or flesh-colored. It has long, narrow wings and a relatively heavy body. In flight, it alternates strong wingbeats with long glides close to the sea surface. Care is needed to separate it from similarly dark shearwaters.
value.rangeHabitat: The Flesh-footed Shearwater breeds on offshore islands in southern Australia, New Zealand, and other parts of the southwestern Pacific, nesting in soil burrows or natural cavities. Outside the breeding season it ranges widely across the Indo-Pacific, using open ocean waters and areas where prey concentrates. In Costa Rica it is exceptionally rare: the first documented record was an individual observed on January 10, 2025, over the Middle America Trench in the Pacific, feeding offshore. It should be regarded as a rare oceanic visitor rather than a regular coastal species.
value.migrationStatus: It is a long-distance migrant. Birds breeding in the South Pacific move northward and widely across the Pacific after breeding. Occurrence in Costa Rica is exceptional and currently documented by a first photographic record from January 10, 2025, in offshore Pacific waters; regular seasonal presence has not been established.
value.breeding: Breeding is colonial and takes place on islands, usually in burrows or other sheltered cavities. Adults generally return to the same breeding areas, and pairs show strong site fidelity. A single egg is laid, and both parents share incubation and chick-rearing. Chicks remain in the burrow until they are fully developed and then depart for the sea. Breeding colonies can be vulnerable because introduced rats, cats, and other predators reach nesting islands and because adults are concentrated in predictable places.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes fish, squid, and other marine animals, especially prey associated with productive ocean fronts, schools of fish, and other feeding aggregations. The species forages by seizing prey at or below the surface and can make shallow dives. It may also scavenge discarded fish or offal around fishing vessels. The Costa Rican individual was observed feeding in a mixed seabird flock associated with spotted dolphins, suggesting localized prey concentration.
value.behavior: Flesh-footed Shearwaters are highly adapted to life at sea, using long glides and strong, efficient flight over open water. They are often gregarious when feeding and may gather with other seabirds and marine mammals. Adults usually approach breeding colonies at night, which reduces exposure to predators. At sea they can travel great distances between feeding areas and nesting islands. Their burrowing lifestyle and strong attachment to breeding colonies make them especially sensitive to disturbance and introduced predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining. Available assessments estimate roughly 148,000 mature individuals, although population estimates remain uncertain for some breeding groups.
conservation.threats: Important threats include accidental capture in commercial longline and other fisheries, introduced predators at breeding colonies, disturbance and habitat degradation on nesting islands, and ingestion of or entanglement in marine plastic. Changes in marine food supplies and climate conditions may also affect breeding success and survival. Because the species concentrates at colonies and overlaps with fisheries, local impacts can have wide population consequences.
conservation.howToHelp: Support fisheries that use effective seabird-bycatch measures, such as night setting, bird-scaring lines, and properly weighted lines. Protect and restore breeding islands by controlling introduced rats, cats, and other predators, and by limiting disturbance during the nesting season. Reduce plastic use and never discard fishing line or other waste at sea. In Costa Rica, reporting and documenting offshore sightings can improve knowledge of this exceptionally rare visitor and its use of Pacific waters.
